::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## The decision this serves
Which structural model can the data support, and what does each parameter in it
physically mean? Get this wrong and every downstream number — the dose
recommendation, the covariate effect, the label — inherits the error.
:::

## 1. A compartment is not an organ

The single most common misconception, and the one that quietly wrecks
interpretation later. A compartment is a **kinetically homogeneous space**: a
mathematical container in which drug is assumed to mix instantaneously and from
which it leaves at a rate proportional to how much is there.

That is all it claims. The "central compartment" is not the blood; the
"peripheral compartment" is not the tissues. They are the smallest number of
containers whose behaviour reproduces what the concentration–time curve does.
PBPK models (`S3`) *do* use compartments that map to real organs — which is
exactly why they need far more parameters and far more *in vitro* data.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
The right way to hold it: **a compartmental model is a description of the
data's behaviour, not a claim about anatomy.** If a two-compartment model fits,
you have learned that the drug leaves the sampled space faster than it is
eliminated — not that you have found a tissue.
:::

## 2. Everything is mass balance

Every equation in pharmacokinetics is the same statement:

$$\frac{dA}{dt} = (\text{rate in}) - (\text{rate out})$$

where $A$ is an amount (mg, µg, µmol), not a concentration. Work in amounts
inside the differential equations and convert to concentration only at the end —
this one habit prevents most unit errors, and `S0-02` is devoted to the rest.

### One compartment, IV bolus

Nothing enters after time zero; drug leaves at a rate proportional to the
amount present:

$$\frac{dA}{dt} = -k \cdot A, \qquad A(0) = D$$

Separate and integrate and you get the exponential decay everyone recognises:

$$A(t) = D e^{-kt}, \qquad C(t) = \frac{D}{V} e^{-kt}$$

Take logs and it is a straight line — which is why the field spent forty years
drawing semi-log plots, and why you should still always look at one.

### Clearance is the primary parameter, not $k$

Here is the conceptual step that separates people who understand PK from people
who can do the algebra.

The elimination rate constant $k$ is a *derived* quantity. What the body
actually does is irreversibly remove drug from a volume of blood per unit time —
that is **clearance**, $CL$, with units of volume/time (L/h). The relationship is

$$k = \frac{CL}{V}, \qquad t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{k} = \frac{0.693 \, V}{CL}$$

Why this matters, concretely: **clearance and volume are physiologically
independent, and $k$ and $t_{1/2}$ are not.** A patient with liver impairment
has lower $CL$. An obese patient may have larger $V$. Both change the half-life,
but they demand *different* dose adjustments — clearance drives the maintenance
dose, volume drives the loading dose. Parameterise a model in $k$ and you have
tangled two mechanisms into one number that no covariate can cleanly explain.

$$\text{maintenance rate} = CL \times C_{ss}, \qquad \text{loading dose} = V \times C_{target}$$

These two lines are most of clinical dose selection.

## 3. Adding absorption

An oral dose does not arrive in the central compartment; it arrives in the gut
and is absorbed. Add a container:

$$\frac{dA_{gut}}{dt} = -k_a A_{gut}, \qquad
\frac{dA_{c}}{dt} = k_a A_{gut} - \frac{CL}{V} A_{c}$$

Two exponentials now shape the curve: absorption in, elimination out. The peak
occurs where they balance,

$$t_{max} = \frac{\ln(k_a / k)}{k_a - k}$$

### The $/F$ problem, and why it is not pedantry

From oral data alone, dose and bioavailability are inseparable — every
observation depends on the product $F \cdot D$. So what you estimate is not
$CL$ and $V$ but $CL/F$ and $V/F$, the *apparent* clearance and volume.

A learner who writes "clearance was 12 L/h" for an oral-only dataset has made a
real error, not a cosmetic one: if $F = 0.4$, true clearance is 4.8 L/h, and any
comparison to hepatic blood flow, to an IV study, or to a PBPK prediction is
now wrong by a factor of two and a half. `CASE-SM` is oral-only for exactly this
reason. Write the `/F`.

### Flip-flop kinetics

When absorption is slower than elimination ($k_a < k$), the terminal slope of
the curve reflects **absorption**, not elimination. The two exponentials swap
roles, the fitted parameters are exchangeable, and a model can converge happily
on the wrong assignment. This is common with extended-release formulations and
with poorly soluble compounds, and the only reliable way to resolve it is IV
data or a formulation comparison — not a better fit statistic.

## 4. Two compartments, and why the curve bends

Plot most real IV data on a semi-log axis and it is not a straight line: there is
a steep early phase, then a shallower one. Drug is distributing into a space
that the sampled compartment exchanges with, and coming back.

$$\frac{dA_c}{dt} = -\frac{CL}{V_c}A_c - \frac{Q}{V_c}A_c + \frac{Q}{V_p}A_p,
\qquad
\frac{dA_p}{dt} = \frac{Q}{V_c}A_c - \frac{Q}{V_p}A_p$$

$Q$ is intercompartmental clearance — the same idea as $CL$, but reversible.
The solution is a sum of two exponentials with hybrid rate constants $\alpha$
(fast, distribution) and $\beta$ (slow, terminal):

$$\alpha, \beta = \tfrac{1}{2}\left[(k_{10}+k_{12}+k_{21}) \pm
\sqrt{(k_{10}+k_{12}+k_{21})^2 - 4k_{10}k_{21}}\right]$$

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**The terminal half-life is not "the" half-life.** For `CASE-SM`, the terminal
$t_{1/2}$ is 14.6 h but the distribution $t_{1/2}$ is 1.85 h, and the drug
accumulates only 1.22-fold on daily dosing — far less than a naive reading of
14.6 h would suggest, because most of the AUC is delivered in the fast phase.
Half-life is a derived, composite quantity. Reason in $CL$ and $V$.
:::

## 5. Why ODEs instead of closed-form solutions

Every model above has an analytical solution, and analytical solutions are much
faster. Use them when you can. But you will abandon them the moment you need any
of the following, which is nearly always:

- **Multiple and irregular doses** — superposition handles repeated identical
  doses, but not missed doses, dose changes, or infusions of varying rate.
- **Nonlinearity** — Michaelis–Menten elimination, target-mediated disposition
  (`S1`), saturable absorption. No closed form exists.
- **Time-varying parameters** — enzyme induction, disease progression, a
  covariate that changes during the study.
- **Anything with feedback** — turnover models, most of PD, all of QSP.

So you learn to write and solve the ODE system, and you keep the analytical
solution as a check on your numerics. Every serious tool in this field —
NONMEM, nlmixr2, Monolix, Pumas, mrgsolve, PK-Sim — is at bottom a
differential-equation solver wrapped in an estimation routine.

### Solving them without lying to yourself

- Use a **stiff-capable solver** (LSODA and friends switch automatically).
  PK/PD systems are routinely stiff — fast absorption alongside slow terminal
  elimination is exactly the condition that makes non-stiff solvers crawl or
  silently lose accuracy.
- **Tighten tolerances until the answer stops moving**, then leave them there.
  Default tolerances are chosen for speed, not for you.
- **Doses are events, not terms in the equation.** Add the amount to the
  compartment at the dose time and restart the integration. Smearing a bolus
  into a continuous input is a classic and hard-to-spot bug.
- **Validate against the analytical solution** whenever one exists. The
  generator for `CASE-SM` was checked exactly this way before the data shipped.

## 6. Linearity buys you one beautiful result

If the system is linear — every rate proportional to an amount — then
superposition holds, and at steady state on a regimen of dose $D$ every $\tau$:

$$AUC_{\tau,ss} = \frac{D}{CL}$$

Exactly. Not approximately, and regardless of how many compartments there are or
what $k_a$ is. For `CASE-SM` at 50 mg with $CL/F = 12$ L/h, that is
4166.7 ng·h/mL, and the numerical solution in the notebook reproduces it to
four figures. It is the cleanest available check that your simulation code is
correct, and it is the reason clearance is the parameter that sets the
maintenance dose.

## Work through it

The notebook builds all of the above from scratch and reproduces every number in
this lesson. Do it in whichever language you are making your primary one.

- [Notebook — R](notebook-r.qmd)
- [Notebook — Python](notebook-py.qmd)

Here is the core of it, side by side:

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```r
library(deSolve)

one_cmt_oral <- function(t, y, p) with(as.list(c(y, p)), {
  dA_gut <- -ka * A_gut
  dA_c   <-  ka * A_gut - (CL / V) * A_c
  list(c(dA_gut, dA_c))
})

p <- c(ka = 1.2, CL = 12, V = 60)          # L/h and L; apparent (X/F)
y0 <- c(A_gut = 50 * 1000, A_c = 0)         # 50 mg as ug -> ug/L reads as ng/mL
out <- ode(y0, seq(0, 48, 0.1), one_cmt_oral, p, method = "lsoda",
           rtol = 1e-9, atol = 1e-12)

conc <- out[, "A_c"] / p["V"]
plot(out[, "time"], conc, type = "l", log = "y",
     xlab = "Time (h)", ylab = "Concentration (ng/mL)")
```

### Python

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

def one_cmt_oral(t, y, ka, CL, V):
    a_gut, a_c = y
    return [-ka * a_gut, ka * a_gut - (CL / V) * a_c]

ka, CL, V = 1.2, 12.0, 60.0                 # L/h and L; apparent (X/F)
y0 = [50 * 1000, 0.0]                       # 50 mg as ug -> ug/L reads as ng/mL
t = np.linspace(0, 48, 481)

sol = solve_ivp(one_cmt_oral, (0, 48), y0, t_eval=t, args=(ka, CL, V),
                method="LSODA", rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-12)
conc = sol.y[1] / V
```

:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Failure mode — fitting structure the data cannot support
Take the `CASE-SM` trough-only samples on days 7, 10 and 21 and try to fit a
two-compartment model to them alone. It will often converge. The standard errors
on $Q$ and $V_p$ will be enormous, the parameters will be strongly correlated,
and the fitted "distribution phase" will be an artefact of three points that
contain no information about distribution at all.

The notebook makes you do this, because the lesson only lands once you have
watched a converged, plausible-looking, meaningless fit come out of your own
code. **Convergence is not evidence.** The diagnostics that catch this —
correlation matrix, condition number, profile likelihood — arrive in `S2`; the
instinct starts here.
:::

## Check yourself

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. A drug's terminal half-life is 40 h. How long until steady state on daily dosing?
You cannot say from that alone, and the question contains a trap. For a
one-compartment drug, roughly 4–5 half-lives — about a week. For a
multi-compartment drug where the 40 h terminal phase carries a small share of
the AUC, the *effective* accumulation half-life is much shorter and the trough
plateaus in days. `CASE-SM` has a 14.6 h terminal half-life and troughs within
5% of steady state by day 4. Compute the accumulation ratio from $AUC_{\tau,ss}
/ AUC_{\tau,1}$; do not read it off the terminal slope.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Why does an oral-only dataset force you to write $CL/F$ rather than $CL$?
Every observed concentration depends on the product $F \cdot D$, so $F$ and the
disposition parameters are structurally unidentifiable — infinitely many
$(F, CL)$ pairs give an identical fit. Only an IV reference arm (or absolute
bioavailability from another source) separates them. The practical damage from
dropping the `/F`: any comparison against hepatic blood flow, against an IV
study, or against a PBPK prediction becomes wrong by the factor $1/F$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Your numerical simulation gives $AUC_{\tau,ss}$ = 4600 ng·h/mL for a 50 mg dose with $CL/F$ = 12 L/h. What is wrong?
Superposition says it must be $D/CL = 50{,}000/12 = 4166.7$ ng·h/mL exactly, for
any linear model. A 10% discrepancy means a bug, not biology. The usual suspects,
in order: not yet at steady state; loose solver tolerances; a unit error between
mg and µg; or dosing implemented as a continuous input rather than as an event.
:::

*Seen in the wild:* a phase 3 dose recommendation was once revisited late
because a model had been parameterised in $k$ and $V$ rather than $CL$ and $V$,
and the renal-impairment covariate had been applied to $k$ — which quietly
changed the volume as well. The fit was fine. The dose adjustment was not.
